Count the white as black

Why the most useful part of a board might be the part you leave empty.

DJ, founderNovember 20266 min read

There’s a small painting at the Met that I go back to more than almost anything else in the building. It’s an album leaf by Ma Yuan, about nine inches square. A scholar sits at the bottom left and looks toward a waterfall. That takes up one corner. The rest of the silk is nearly empty: some mist and a lot of nothing.

The first time I saw it I thought it was unfinished. By the fifth time I’d figured out that the empty part was what I kept coming back for.

I think about that leaf a lot while building Nook, because the question I keep running into isn’t how to help people hold more. It’s closer to the opposite.

One corner

Ma Yuan painted for the Southern Song court around 1200. He and Xia Gui, who worked at the same time, picked up nicknames that have stuck for eight hundred years: Ma One-Corner and Xia Half-Side (马一角，夏半边). They pushed the mountains, the trees and the people into one corner or one half of the picture and left the rest open.

Put that next to what came a century before. Guo Xi’s Early Spring, painted in 1072, is a wall of mountain. Every inch of the scroll is busy with ridges, mist, pines clawing at rock, little buildings, tiny travelers. It’s magnificent. It’s also tiring in the way a full inbox is tiring. Your eye never gets to rest, because there’s nowhere to set it down.

Some later critics read Ma’s empty corners as a portrait of a shrunken empire. The Song had lost the north, and here were court painters who could only fill a corner. I think that misses what the painters knew. The emptiness isn’t something missing. It’s where the viewer gets to stand.

Count the white as black

Chinese calligraphers have a phrase for this, usually credited to the Qing master Deng Shiru: 计白当黑, count the white as black. The blank paper is part of the composition, as deliberate as the ink.

The idea is far older than painting. Chapter 11 of the Tao Te Ching makes the case with three ordinary objects. Thirty spokes share one hub, and the empty center is what makes the wheel turn. You shape clay into a pot, and the hollow inside is what holds the water. You cut doors and windows into walls, and the room is useful because of the space they enclose.

Twenty-five centuries later it’s still the best product spec I know for a place to think.

A room the size of four things

Here’s where it stops being about art.

In 1956 the psychologist George Miller published a paper with one of the great titles in science, “The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two.” It argued that we can keep about seven things in mind at once. Later work, most influentially Nelson Cowan’s in 2001, put the real number closer to four.

Four. That’s the size of the room you think in. Everything else you’re keeping track of is either crowding into that room or living somewhere outside your head.

Herbert Simon saw where this was going in 1971, long before anyone carried a phone: “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.” Information eats attention, so more of one means less of the other. Nearly every app on your home screen is on the far side of that trade.

So the question I ask of any tool that holds my thinking is how much of that four-thing room it leaves open.

Deciding is what makes room

Marie Kondo gets reduced to folding T-shirts into thirds, which is a shame, because her real point is about decisions. Her method is a long series of decisions about what you’re keeping, and the space shows up as a side effect of the deciding.

That’s the strange arithmetic of organizing. Done well, it gives you space back. You choose what belongs together and where it lives, and then you never have to hold it in your head again.

The cognitive scientist David Kirsh spent years watching people do this without noticing. In a 1995 paper called “The Intelligent Use of Space,” he studied cooks laying out ingredients, people bagging groceries, workers arranging parts. His argument was that the way we arrange things around us is part of how we think, not housekeeping that happens afterward. Putting the chopped onions to the left of the stove is a way of remembering what comes next without having to remember it.

Otto’s notebook

In 1998 the philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers published a short paper called “The Extended Mind.” Its best-known example happens to be a New York story.

Inga hears there’s an exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art. She thinks for a second, remembers that the museum is on 53rd Street, and walks there. Otto has Alzheimer’s. He carries a notebook everywhere and writes down what he learns. He hears about the same exhibition, opens the notebook, reads “53rd Street,” and walks there too.

Clark and Chalmers asked whether Otto’s notebook is any less a part of his mind than Inga’s memory is of hers. They said no. If something outside your head is reliably there and does the job memory would do, it’s part of how you think.

I find that idea moving, and also practical. If your notebook is part of your mind, then the shape of the notebook becomes the shape of your thinking. One endless list thinks like a list. A surface with room on it, where things sit near the things they belong with, thinks a little more like a painting.

The studio wall

When Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi began studying creativity in the 1960s, he spent time with art students. What struck him was how completely they disappeared into a painting while they worked, and how fast they lost interest once it was done. The doing was the point. He later called that state flow.

Walk into almost any working studio and you’ll see the other half of flow pinned to the wall: sketches, photos, swatches, a postcard from somewhere. The wall is what lets the artist stop carrying everything at once and get into the work. It sits between everything they’ve ever seen and the one canvas in front of them.

Most of us never had a wall like that for the things we’re actually in the middle of. A move. A trip. A stuck chapter. We had tabs.

Why a nook

So that’s why I’m building Nook, and why it’s small on purpose.

A nook is the corner of a room you set aside for one thing, like the reading chair or the desk by the window. You don’t put everything there. You put the few things you’re living with right now, and you leave room around them.

At its best, a board is Ma Yuan’s leaf. What matters sits together in one corner, close to the things it belongs with, and the rest stays white, so your eye and that small four-thing room both get somewhere to rest. The white isn’t wasted. Count it as black.

I still go and see the waterfall. The scholar is still sitting there, looking at something we can’t quite make out, with most of the silk left open for us. It’s one of the calmest places in New York.
